paragraphs: Methods for improving fairness in machine learning often address different versions of the problem. They may intervene at different stages, handle different combinations of sensitive features, or use different definitions of fairness. These differences make direct comparisons difficult: even methods intended for binary classification can share only a narrow set of compatible settings.

ABCFair approaches benchmarking as something that should adapt to the requirements of the application. Rather than assuming that every fairness method solves an identical problem, it organizes comparisons around the desired problem setting. The contribution is therefore a flexible approach to evaluation, helping make comparisons relevant to the conditions under which a method would actually be used.

The authors apply the benchmark to methods that act before, during, and after model training. Their evaluation includes large traditional datasets and a dataset containing both biased and unbiased labels, which they use to sidestep the fairness–accuracy trade-off. The abstract presents this adaptable comparison framework and its application, without identifying a single fairness method as the overall winner.
neurips-2024-abcfair-an-adaptable-benchm.tldr: ABCFair adapts fairness benchmarking to an application's requirements so methods addressing different settings can be compared meaningfully.

paragraphs: A neural network can appear to acquire a new ability suddenly as training time, available data, or model size increases. This paper studies that emergence through a simplified mathematical model. It represents each skill as a basis function, giving the analysis an explicit way to describe which abilities the model has learned and how they develop.

Within this representation, the authors solve a simple multilinear model. They derive analytic expressions for skill emergence and for how loss changes with training time, dataset size, model size, and optimal compute. This connects the appearance of individual abilities with broader scaling behavior inside one tractable framework, rather than treating them as unrelated observations.

The authors compare these calculations with simulations of a two-layer neural network trained on multitask sparse parity, with task frequencies following a power law. Using one fitted parameter, the simplified model captures the network's S-shaped acquisition of multiple skills as resources increase. The result supports the model's explanatory value in this particular setting; its evidence concerns the stated task distribution and neural-network experiments.
neurips-2024-an-exactly-solvable-model-f.tldr: An exactly solvable skill-based model captures emergence and loss scaling in neural networks trained on multitask sparse parity.

paragraphs: Personalized image generation must preserve a user-provided subject while following new textual instructions. The paper examines two established personalization techniques and identifies different difficulties. Textual Inversion tends to overfit the learned concept when it appears in new prompts, while DreamBooth often gives that concept too little attention. Both behaviors interfere with flexible, faithful personalization.

The authors attribute these problems to incorrectly learned alignment of the concept's embedding. AttnDreamBooth responds by dividing training into stages that separately learn embedding alignment, the attention map, and subject identity. This separation gives each component a distinct learning stage within the overall personalization process. The method also adds a regularization term specifically intended to improve cross-attention map learning.

The reported results show significant improvements over the baseline methods in both preserving identity and matching the text. These findings matter because the two goals must work together: recognizing the personalized subject is insufficient if the generated image does not follow the prompt. The paper's contribution is a staged training approach that improves this joint behavior in its comparisons.
neurips-2024-attndreambooth-towards-text.tldr: AttnDreamBooth separates alignment, attention, and identity learning to improve personalized image generation's subject fidelity and prompt adherence.

paragraphs: Inverse protein folding seeks amino-acid sequences that will fold into a desired backbone structure. The paper argues that prevailing discriminative approaches can accumulate errors and struggle to represent the many sequences that could plausibly fit a structure. Bridge-IF instead treats sequence design as a generative process linking backbone structures with a distribution of possible protein sequences.

A structure encoder first proposes an informative initial sequence distribution. A Markov bridge connects this structure-derived starting point to native sequences during learning. At inference, the model progressively refines an initial sequence into a more plausible design. Starting from structural information makes the refinement process directly responsive to the backbone that the designed protein should match.

The authors also derive a simpler training loss through a reparameterization of the bridge model. They condition protein language models on structure to approximate the bridge while keeping training parameter-efficient. On established benchmarks, Bridge-IF surpasses existing baselines in most sequence-recovery comparisons and performs strongly at designing plausible, highly foldable proteins. These findings support both recovering native sequence information and generating structurally suitable designs.
neurips-2024-bridge-if-learning-inverse-.tldr: Bridge-IF progressively refines structure-informed protein sequences through a Markov bridge, improving sequence recovery and plausible protein design.

paragraphs: DenoiseRep applies denoising to learning features useful for prediction, rather than focusing on generating data. Its goal is to improve how well a model's internal representations distinguish relevant information. The central idea is to combine feature extraction with feature cleanup throughout the backbone, so representations become more useful as they pass through successive layers.

The method treats each embedding layer as a denoising step. This connects two progressive processes: moving from lower-level to higher-level features and repeatedly removing noise from those features. It then merges the parameters used for extraction and denoising. The authors theoretically establish equivalence before and after this fusion, allowing the denoising operation to be incorporated without separate computational overhead.

DenoiseRep does not require labels, although it can complement label-based learning when labels are available. Experiments report consistent improvements across re-identification, classification, object detection, and image segmentation, using both convolutional and Transformer architectures. This breadth supports the approach as a general feature-learning addition within the evaluated settings, while the parameter fusion makes its computational contribution especially relevant for prediction models.
neurips-2024-denoiserep-denoising-model-.tldr: DenoiseRep improves visual representations by combining feature extraction with denoising and fusing their parameters to avoid separate denoising computation.

paragraphs: Generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting reconstructs unfamiliar scenes from a small number of views without retraining separately for each scene. Existing approaches often rely on epipolar constraints to connect observations across images. The paper highlights a difficulty with that reliance: those constraints can become unreliable where views do not overlap or scene content is hidden by occlusion.

eFreeSplat produces a scene representation through feed-forward inference without imposing epipolar line constraints. It uses a self-supervised Vision Transformer pretrained on cross-view completion to extract features with stronger awareness of three-dimensional structure. An iterative alignment procedure then coordinates Gaussians across views, addressing differences in their depth scales so the combined reconstruction uses consistent spatial information.

The authors evaluate the method on wide-baseline novel-view synthesis using RealEstate10K and ACID. They report better geometry reconstruction and synthesized-view quality than state-of-the-art baselines that depend on epipolar priors. The findings show that the proposed learned cross-view features and alignment can outperform those explicitly constrained alternatives in the evaluated tasks, while retaining reconstruction without scene-specific retraining.
neurips-2024-epipolar-free-3d-gaussian-s.tldr: eFreeSplat reconstructs scenes and synthesizes new views without epipolar constraints, using learned cross-view features and iterative Gaussian alignment.

paragraphs: A generated video can contain actions that are difficult to judge using assessment methods developed for real, standardized activities. This paper treats the visual rationality of generated actions as a distinct evaluation problem. It argues that methods trained around normative action features do not adequately handle the ambiguous actions found in AI-generated videos.

The authors build GAIA through a large subjective evaluation organized around causal reasoning. The dataset contains 971,244 ratings covering 9,180 video-action pairs. They use it to compare popular text-to-video models across action categories, revealing different strengths and weaknesses. They also turn it into a testbed for whether automatic evaluation methods agree with human judgments of action quality.

Traditional action assessment methods, action-related text-to-video metrics, and general video-quality methods achieve average rank correlations of 0.454, 0.191, and 0.519, respectively. The authors interpret these results as a substantial gap between existing evaluation systems and human perception. GAIA therefore contributes both human-rated evidence for comparing generators and a benchmark for developing assessments that better capture generated action quality.
neurips-2024-gaia-rethinking-action-qual.tldr: GAIA benchmarks action quality in AI-generated videos and reveals substantial gaps between existing automatic assessments and human judgments.

paragraphs: Predicting human movement involves uncertainty because several future motions may be plausible. But a person's surroundings also impose constraints on where and how they can move. This paper introduces the task of predicting diverse human motions inside real-world 3D scenes, addressing artifacts that arise when motion prediction emphasizes variability while neglecting the physical environment.

The proposed DiMoP3D framework takes a scene point cloud together with observed movement. It uses that history to infer likely target objects and the poses needed to interact with them. It then plans an obstacle-free route toward those objects and generates multiple possible future motions. Scene understanding therefore shapes both the intended interaction and the movement leading to it.

DiMoP3D incorporates deterministic environmental factors into its stochastic generation process, making variation responsive to the scene. On two benchmarks captured in real environments, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining diversity with physical consistency: the model aims to preserve multiple plausible futures while making those futures compatible with the surrounding 3D environment.
neurips-2024-harmonizing-stochasticity-a.tldr: DiMoP3D combines scene constraints with stochastic prediction to generate diverse, physically consistent human motions in real 3D environments.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision methods often learn from multiple augmented versions of an image, but their practical designs rely on many heuristics. This paper builds on theory connecting different frameworks to the same idealized objective: learning features that match the similarity structure induced by those augmentations. That shared perspective provides a basis for more systematic training choices.

The authors reformulate the idealized objective into a functionally equivalent loss that is cheaper to compute. Their analysis of gradient descent suggests combining a stronger orthogonalization constraint with a smaller projector dimension. It also indicates that using more augmentations improves the approximation of the reformulated objective, providing a theoretical reason to expect better convergence from additional views.

Experiments on CIFAR, STL, and ImageNet support these recommendations through improved linear-readout performance with a ResNet backbone. The authors also report maintaining downstream accuracy while reducing the pretraining dataset size by up to a factor of two through additional augmentations. These results show how choices about projector size and views can improve the use of available training data in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-harnessing-small-projectors.tldr: Theory-guided use of smaller projectors, stronger orthogonalization, and more augmented views improves self-supervised vision pretraining efficiency.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be demanding to deploy, especially when available hardware varies between devices or over time. One response is to train and store separate models at several sizes, but that creates its own burden. HydraViT instead develops a scalable model whose internal subnetworks provide different choices of computational cost within one trained architecture.

The approach stacks attention heads and repeatedly changes embedding dimensions and the corresponding number of attention heads during training. These changes induce multiple subnetworks with different resource requirements. Training across these configurations is intended to preserve useful performance throughout the range, allowing the architecture to adapt to hardware constraints through the available subnetwork choices.

Experiments demonstrate a model with up to ten subnetworks. On ImageNet-1K, HydraViT achieves gains of up to five percentage points in accuracy at the same GMAC count and up to seven percentage points at the same throughput compared with the baselines. These are reported maximum improvements, supporting the usefulness of a scalable Transformer for the evaluated resource constraints.
neurips-2024-hydravit-stacking-heads-for.tldr: HydraViT trains multiple resource-scaled subnetworks within one Vision Transformer by varying embedding dimensions and attention-head counts.

paragraphs: Foundation models contain useful information across modalities, but combining their representations into a shared system requires alignment. FIND introduces a lightweight Transformer interface that connects those embeddings while leaving the foundation models' weights unchanged. The aim is to support understanding at different levels, from regions within an image to relationships across a dataset.

The interface supports segmentation, grounding, and retrieval through the same architecture and weights. Multitask, multimodal training creates a shared embedding space in which these capabilities can be interleaved. The authors also describe the interface as extendable to new models and tasks. This makes the alignment layer the central mechanism for coordinating existing model capabilities across different forms of input and output.

To evaluate this combined behavior, the paper introduces FIND-Bench, adding training and evaluation annotations to COCO for interleaved segmentation and retrieval. FIND achieves state-of-the-art performance on that benchmark and competitive results on standard retrieval and segmentation settings. The distinction matters: its strongest reported result concerns the new benchmark designed around the interface's combined capabilities.
neurips-2024-interfacing-foundation-mode.tldr: FIND aligns frozen foundation-model embeddings through a lightweight interface that jointly supports segmentation, grounding, and retrieval.

paragraphs: CLIP classifies an image without task-specific training by comparing its representation with textual representations of candidate classes. The closest class representation becomes the prediction. This paper asks what makes those representations close in the first place: which concepts are shared by CLIP's image and language encoders, and how does that shared knowledge influence classification?

The authors develop explanations expressed through textual concepts. Their focus is the knowledge common to both modalities, because that commonality helps explain relationships in the joint embedding space. This gives a more interpretable account of a prediction than proximity alone: it seeks to describe the concepts associated with why image and class representations are positioned together or apart.

The analysis covers thirteen CLIP models with different architectures, sizes, and pretraining datasets. It examines how these differences relate to mutual knowledge and uses the resulting explanations to analyze zero-shot predictions. The authors report that the approach is effective and accessible to people. Its contribution is an explanatory view of CLIP's decisions, together with a comparative analysis across the model pool.
neurips-2024-interpreting-and-analysing-.tldr: The paper explains CLIP's zero-shot classifications through textual concepts shared by its image and language encoders.

paragraphs: Reconstructing and understanding a scene from a few images often involves several stages, including camera estimation, geometric reconstruction, and task-specific analysis. Large Spatial Model combines these operations into a single feed-forward system. It accepts RGB images without supplied camera poses and jointly estimates scene geometry, appearance, and semantics as a semantic radiance field.

A Transformer framework predicts global geometry through point maps aligned with image pixels. Local context aggregation and multiscale fusion improve the representation of fine details. To address limited labeled 3D semantic data, the model incorporates a pretrained language-based 2D segmentation model into a spatially consistent semantic feature field. A decoder expresses the result as semantic anisotropic Gaussians for end-to-end supervised learning.

The resulting representation supports language interaction and the synthesis of label maps from new viewpoints. Experiments across several tasks show that LSM can bring multiple 3D vision capabilities into one pipeline operating directly on unposed images. The authors report real-time semantic 3D reconstruction, making processing speed and integrated scene understanding central outcomes of the approach.
neurips-2024-large-spatial-model-end-to-.tldr: Large Spatial Model converts unposed images into geometry, appearance, and language-accessible 3D semantics in one feed-forward pass.

paragraphs: Concept activation vectors connect a model's predictions to recognizable concepts, making them useful for explaining model behavior. Training them typically requires carefully curated images, which limits which concepts can be studied. LG-CAV replaces that labeled-image requirement with language guidance drawn from a pretrained vision-language model, using a concept's description to guide the learning process.

The method connects the vision-language model to the target model through a common pool of probe images. It measures how strongly each image activates the described concept in the vision-language model, then uses those values to train a concept vector for the target model. The probe pool provides a shared reference even though the two models have different internal representations.

The paper also introduces activation sample reweighting, which uses learned concepts associated with the target model's predicted classes to improve that model. Across four datasets and nine architectures, the authors report substantially higher concept-vector quality than previous methods and state-of-the-art correction performance among concept-based approaches. The results support using language-derived concept knowledge for both interpretation and model improvement.
neurips-2024-lg-cav-train-any-concept-ac.tldr: LG-CAV learns concept activation vectors from language-guided probe images without labeled concept data and uses them to improve target models.

paragraphs: Long-tailed object detection must learn categories that appear frequently alongside others with very few examples. The paper identifies severe data imbalance and simplicity bias as obstacles for pretraining in this setting. Its proposed framework, 2DRCL, changes the pretraining process to give underrepresented categories better representation while learning features suited to locating and recognizing objects.

The framework combines three components. Holistic-local contrastive learning captures both broad scene context and detailed local patterns, bringing pretraining closer to the needs of detection. Dynamic rebalancing changes how underrepresented instances are sampled throughout training. Dual reconstruction adds a self-consistency-based reconstruction task intended to address simplicity bias, with particular benefit for the rare categories in the distribution.

Experiments on COCO and LVIS v1.0 demonstrate improvements, especially in the reported mAP and AP results for tail classes. These findings connect the method's design to its intended outcome: better detection of categories that receive relatively little data. The contribution is the combined pretraining framework, addressing feature scale, sampling imbalance, and reconstruction together.
neurips-2024-long-tailed-object-detectio.tldr: 2DRCL combines global-local contrastive learning, dynamic sampling, and dual reconstruction to improve detection of underrepresented object categories.

paragraphs: MetaUAS investigates whether a purely visual foundation model can locate unfamiliar anomalies without language prompts. Its central move is to reformulate anomaly segmentation as change segmentation. A normal image supplies the reference, and the model identifies anomalous regions in a query image through its learned ability to perceive differences between paired images.

The authors train a one-prompt meta-learning framework on synthetic image pairs created from existing datasets. These pairs contain changes to entire objects and to local regions, without depending on the target anomaly datasets. A soft feature alignment module handles geometric differences between the reference and query, connecting paired-image change perception with the segmentation of regions within an individual image.

After this training, MetaUAS uses one normal image as its prompt without further training or language guidance. The authors report strong generalization to unseen anomalies and significant improvements over previous zero-shot, few-shot, and even full-shot methods. The approach matters because its preparation relies on synthetic visual changes, while its use requires only a normal visual example of the target setting.
neurips-2024-metauas-universal-anomaly-s.tldr: MetaUAS learns anomaly segmentation from synthetic visual changes and identifies unseen anomalies using a single normal-image prompt.

paragraphs: High-dimensional data can make private analysis expensive, even when the data largely occupy a much smaller subspace. Privately finding that subspace could reduce the burden of the surrounding dimensions. However, general lower bounds show that private subspace estimation can require a number of points growing polynomially with dimension, leaving open which easier datasets might avoid that cost.

This paper introduces measures of easiness based on multiplicative gaps between singular values of the input data. These gaps describe separations within the data's spectral structure. The authors develop both upper and lower bounds around those measures, identifying types of gaps that are sufficient and necessary for estimating a subspace with a number of points independent of ambient dimension.

They also implement the upper-bound results through a practical algorithm and demonstrate advantages over previous approaches in high-dimensional settings. The key qualification is that dimension-independent estimation is tied to the identified gap conditions. The work therefore characterizes favorable instances within a distribution-free setting while preserving the general difficulty of private subspace estimation.
neurips-2024-on-differentially-private-s.tldr: The paper characterizes singular-value gaps that enable dimension-independent private subspace estimation and provides a practical algorithm.

paragraphs: Multiobjective optimization seeks useful trade-offs among several goals. Scalarization combines those goals into one objective, but linear combinations cannot explore concave portions of the Pareto frontier. This paper studies simple nonlinear scalarizations designed to cover diverse trade-offs, measuring their quality through dominated hypervolume, which captures how much objective-space volume the obtained solutions dominate.

The authors prove that hypervolume scalarizations with uniformly random weights achieve a regret bound of O(T^(-1/k)) for k objectives. Matching lower bounds establish that no algorithm can improve the asymptotic rate under the analyzed setting. This gives the proposed scalarization strategy a guarantee about the quality of its coverage, beyond its convenience as a way to combine objectives.

For multiobjective stochastic linear bandits, a non-Euclidean analysis yields a bound of Õ(d T^(-1/2) + T^(-1/k)), removing unnecessary polynomial dependence on the number of objectives. Experiments also show strong performance against linear scalarizations and standard multiobjective algorithms across several settings. Together, the theory and empirical results support nonlinear scalarization as an effective approach to exploring objective trade-offs.
neurips-2024-optimal-scalarizations-for-.tldr: Randomly weighted nonlinear hypervolume scalarizations achieve an asymptotically optimal regret rate for exploring multiple objectives.

paragraphs: PromptFix addresses two challenges in instruction-driven image processing: insufficient diversity in training instructions and loss of fine image detail during diffusion-based editing. The framework aims to support a broad range of requested changes while preserving details in areas that do not need processing. Its scope includes low-level image tasks, editing, and object creation.

The authors first construct a large instruction-following dataset spanning these tasks. They then introduce a sampling method that guides denoising with high-frequency information, explicitly helping preserve fine details in untouched regions. An auxiliary prompting adapter uses vision-language models to enrich text prompts and improve generalization. The three components address training coverage, image preservation, and interpretation of the requested task.

Experiments report better performance than previous methods across multiple image-processing tasks, with comparable inference efficiency. PromptFix also shows stronger zero-shot performance on blind restoration and combination tasks. These findings suggest that broader instruction data, targeted sampling guidance, and enhanced prompts can work together to improve both task flexibility and preservation of the original image's relevant details.
neurips-2024-promptfix-you-prompt-and-we.tldr: PromptFix combines diverse instruction training, detail-preserving diffusion guidance, and enhanced prompts for flexible image processing.

paragraphs: When test labels are unavailable, it is difficult to judge whether a predictor learned from training data remains suitable for the test distribution. Importance Divergence, or I-Div, addresses this by transferring test-distribution sampling patterns onto training data. This lets the discrepancy evaluation operate on training samples while incorporating information about how test inputs are distributed.

The method estimates two linked quantities: a density ratio and a likelihood ratio. The density-ratio estimate depends on the selected hypothesis and is learned by minimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between actual and estimated input distributions. The likelihood ratio is adjusted in relation to that density ratio by reducing the generalization error of the discrepancy transformed through both ratios.

This construction makes distribution comparison sensitive to the hypothesis being assessed and avoids requiring test class labels. Across a broad range of complex data scenarios and tasks, the authors report that I-Div accurately quantifies distribution discrepancy. The stated contribution is a way to evaluate the mismatch through sampling transfer, helping address the uncertainty surrounding the applicability of a training-selected predictor.
neurips-2024-revealing-distribution-disc.tldr: I-Div estimates train–test distribution discrepancy without test labels by transferring test sampling patterns onto training data through learned ratios.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation requires a model to interpret a visual scene, reason about a task, and produce an action. RoboMamba addresses both reasoning limitations and the computational cost of existing vision-language-action models. It builds on Mamba, a state-space sequence model with linear inference complexity, to combine these capabilities in an end-to-end robotic system.

The authors first connect a vision encoder to Mamba and jointly train them to align visual tokens with language embeddings. This stage develops visual common sense and robot-related reasoning. They then add a simple policy head and use an efficient fine-tuning strategy for predicting three-dimensional position and orientation. Their finding is conditional: once reasoning is sufficiently developed, manipulation skills can be learned by fine-tuning only 0.1% of the model.

Experiments report strong reasoning performance on general and robotic benchmarks, alongside pose-prediction results in simulation and the real world. RoboMamba also achieves inference speeds three times those of the compared VLA models. The results connect a reasoning-capable backbone with economical action adaptation and faster inference in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-robomamba-efficient-vision-.tldr: RoboMamba combines visual-language reasoning with efficient robotic pose prediction, reporting minimal action fine-tuning and faster inference.

paragraphs: Jailbreaking attacks modify prompts to make language models behave in unwanted ways. The paper argues that defenses need to account for attackers who adapt, including attacks beyond those already considered during development. Robust Prompt Optimization, or RPO, addresses this by placing the adversary directly inside the objective used to construct a system-level defense.

RPO optimizes a lightweight, transferable suffix rather than relying only on a fixed manually designed instruction. Because the defensive objective explicitly incorporates adversarial behavior, the method is designed to adapt to worst-case adaptive attacks. The central contribution is the combination of this optimization objective and an algorithm that turns it into a prompt-based defensive component.

The authors present theoretical and experimental results supporting improved robustness against both attacks encountered during optimization and previously unknown jailbreaks. On JailbreakBench, they report attack success rates of 6% for GPT-4 and 0% for Llama-2, achieving state-of-the-art results in that evaluation. These figures describe benchmark outcomes; the zero rate is a result for the tested attacks, rather than a universal guarantee.
neurips-2024-robust-prompt-optimization-.tldr: RPO optimizes a transferable defensive prompt suffix against an explicit adversary, improving jailbreak resistance on JailbreakBench.

paragraphs: Combining images from different modalities can preserve complementary information, but degraded inputs may carry noise, color bias, and exposure problems into the fused result. Objects that matter to a user may also become less prominent. Text-DiFuse addresses both issues with a diffusion-based fusion framework that accepts textual control over the resulting image.

The method integrates information at the feature level within the diffusion process, combining degradation removal with multimodal fusion. It also joins text guidance with a zero-shot localization model to modify the fusion process around the user's interests. This lets a textual request help emphasize foreground objects, connecting the visual combination process with the content the user wants to highlight.

Across public datasets with complex degradations, the authors report state-of-the-art fusion performance in varied scenarios. A semantic segmentation experiment also shows a significant improvement from the text-controlled re-modulation strategy. That result supports the usefulness of textual control beyond appearance alone: emphasizing relevant content also improves the reported semantic evaluation of the fused images.
neurips-2024-text-difuse-an-interactive-.tldr: Text-DiFuse combines multimodal fusion and degradation removal within diffusion, using text guidance to emphasize objects of interest.

paragraphs: Federated Q-learning lets several agents collaborate to learn the optimal action-value function of an unknown environment. This paper studies an infinite-horizon Markov decision process with finite state and action spaces. Its central question is how much communication agents must use to obtain the sample-efficiency benefits of collaboration when they exchange information only intermittently.

The authors first establish a lower bound: achieving a linear improvement in sample complexity with the number of agents requires communication cost of at least Ω(1/(1−γ)), where γ is the discount factor. This ties the minimum communication burden to the importance of future rewards. As the discount factor approaches one, that lower bound increases.

They then introduce Fed-DVR-Q, which simultaneously achieves order-optimal sample and communication complexities. The algorithm supplies the achievable side of the result, while the lower bound identifies a cost that successful methods cannot avoid in the analyzed setting. Together, these establish the sample–communication trade-off for the studied class of federated Q-learning algorithms, clarifying when additional agents can deliver proportional sampling benefits.
neurips-2024-the-sample-communication-co.tldr: The paper proves a communication lower bound for sample-efficient federated Q-learning and introduces Fed-DVR-Q to attain optimal orders of both costs.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset, which may contain corrupted states, actions, rewards, or dynamics. Such corruption can undermine the learned agent even when it is later evaluated in a clean environment. TRACER addresses these different corruption types through a common representation: uncertainty in the action-value function learned from the offline data.

The method uses all offline observations to approximate a posterior distribution over the action-value function through variational Bayesian inference. It then measures uncertainty using entropy. The reasoning is that corrupted observations often produce greater uncertainty and entropy, allowing the method to distinguish them from cleaner observations. This is a tendency used by the approach, rather than an assertion that every corrupted sample is always identifiable.

TRACER uses the uncertainty measure to regulate the loss associated with corrupted data, reducing its influence during learning. Experiments report significant improvements over several state-of-the-art methods under both individual and simultaneous corruption types. The findings support uncertainty-aware training as a way to improve robustness and subsequent performance in clean environments despite contaminated offline experience.
neurips-2024-uncertainty-based-offline-v.tldr: TRACER uses Bayesian value-function uncertainty to reduce the influence of corrupted offline reinforcement-learning data.
